paragraphs.text: A [tuo](sheng:pressing) of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) made in 1996 from leaf grown in [Menghai County](menghai-county:county-and-factory), Yunnan. Tea was first pressed into compact shapes like this small bowl so it could travel the old trade routes, and the shape still decides how it ages: a small tuo changes faster than a large, tight cake.

It was made in the years when [collectors](sheng:history-modern), led at first by Taiwan, came looking for aged raw pu’er. At thirty years it is past both lines the trade draws for [aged](sheng:ageing) raw tea, ten years for some and twenty or more for many. Raw pu’er gets no quick fermentation, so it [changes slowly in storage](sheng:aging). How warm and humid its [stores](sheng:storage) were over those three decades is part of its history, as much as the years themselves.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
